newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists propose 35-hour working week.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists propose 35-hour working week.

text.p: France's opposition Socialist Party will promise to cut the working week to 35 hours and create 700,000 jobs for young people at a cost of about 50 billion francs ($8.6 billion), party policy-maker Dominique Strauss-Kahn said on Friday.

The Socialists are due to unveil their manifesto for the May 25-June 1 parliamentary election later on Friday. Strauss-Kahn said in a newspaper interview his party would propose reducing the working week by law within three years.

Strauss-Kahn told the business daily La Tribune that the Socialists wanted to create 350,000 public sector jobs by getting local authorities to offer young people five-year contracts on a full-time basis, paying at least the national minimum wage.

This plan would cost around 35 billion francs, he said. The state would finance these jobs where it was a direct employer or else foot 80 percent of the bill, with some of the money coming from the scrapping of certain employment incentive schemes.
It would propose subsidies to help create another 350,000 jobs in the private sector at a cost of around 15 billion francs, he said.

Strauss-Kahn, co-author of Socialist economic policy, said his party was committed to going ahead with European monetary union as planned at the start of 1999 but that the future single currency, the euro, should not simply be an end in itself.
"Nothing would be worse than making this move without the European people feeling the slightest improvement in their situation," he said.
"If the euro is to serve a purpose, it should not be overvalued against the dollar on the one hand and it should also contribute to stimulating the economy and employment."

Strauss-Kahn, whose party trails the ruling centre-right coalition in opinion polls on the likely winners of the snap general election, said the jobs plan was not intended to boost the number of civil servants in France's central administration.

On shortening the working week, Strauss-Kahn said the aim was to push for a shorter working week over a period of three years and then introduce legislation reducing the work week to 35 hours across the board.
Employers would be encouraged to go even further, with help from the state if they adopted a 32-hour week, he said.

Fighting unemployment, which is stuck at a record 12.8 percent despite slight falls in the number out of work in February and March, is one of the key themes of the Socialist campaign, coupled with plans to boost consumer spending power.
